sbh1.3:1.0: The source has *naiṣkramyabhūmiḥ naiṣkramyabhūmiḥ katamā* — the bhūmi name repeated, with no Roman-numeral marker. Treated here as 'name + question': the first occurrence (now :1.0) functions as the section header (as Roman-numeral *I.* and *II.* did in [sbh1.1](sbh1.1.html) and [sbh1.2](sbh1.2.html)), the second (now :1.1) as the standard *X katamā* opening question. The Roman numeral *III.* has been editorially restored in brackets — the dittographic doubling of *naiṣkramyabhūmiḥ* in the source likely covers a lost *III.* marker, since the section is the third sub-bhūmi of Yogasthāna I in clear continuity with the *I.*/*II.* pattern of the preceding two.
sbh1.3:1.8: *samāpatti-upapattika dhyāna* — the dhyāna treated under both its aspects: as a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) reached in this life, and as a corresponding mode of rebirth (*upapatti*) into the dhyāna-heaven of the same name. This dual reference is canonical: the same term names both the practice and the cosmological-rebirth realm it leads to.
sbh1.3:1.9: *satkāya-vairāgyam* — 'dispassion toward the personality.' In context, the practitioner attains dispassion specifically toward the *kāmadhātu*-bound personality — the embodied-self of the desire realm — which is the precondition for transitioning into the first dhyāna. *Satkāya* (literally 'existing body / aggregates') is the same term that grounds *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (identity-view).
sbh1.3:1.21: *darśana-bhāvanā-prahātavyebhyo dharmebhyaḥ* — 'the dharmas to be abandoned by vision and by cultivation.' Refers to the canonical two-stage path of the *darśana-mārga* (path of seeing, which abandons the intellectually-grasped defilements at first true insight) and the *bhāvanā-mārga* (path of cultivation, which gradually wears down the residual affective defilements). Together these constitute the supramundane path proper.
sbh1.3:2.3: The list enumerates the thirteen *saṁbhāra* (requisites) that the rest of this chapter unpacks. The extracted root here skips directly from *śīla-saṁvara* to *bhojane mātrajñatā*, but the closing *uddāna* at 80.1 has *śīlendriya-* and the chapter itself devotes 32.1–35.65 to *indriya-saṁvara*; English therefore supplies sense-faculty restraint in brackets. *Kalyāṇamitratā* (association with good friends) appears in this enumeration but is folded into [*parasampat*](sbh1.1.html#sbh1.1:1.26) in the gotrabhūmi treatment, hence its absence from the closing verse.
sbh1.3:2.5: Cross-reference back to [sbh1.1:10.20–21](sbh1.1.html#sbh1.1:10.20), the gotrabhūmi treatment of *ātmasampat*, *parasampat*, and *kuśala-dharma-cchanda* under the rubric of the lesser supporting condition for the perfecting of the lineage-seed. The avatārabhūmi does not re-define these three; the present chapter inherits them and proceeds directly to the fourth requisite (*śīla-saṁvara*) at 2.6.
sbh1.3:82.1: The closing *uddāna* (summary verse) is in *śloka* meter; English here drops the meter and adds bracketed clarifications so the verse remains a list-pointer rather than a freestanding statement. Verses 82–83 enumerate the twelve saṁbhāras of the chapter (with *kalyāṇamitratā* implicit under *parasampat*); verses 84–85 enumerate the qualities of the recluse-ornament treated in sections 73–80.
sbh1.3:3.2: *sapta-naiḥsaraṇika śīla-skandha* — the seven categories of virtue conducive to liberation (*naiḥsaraṇika*, 'leading-out'). The Yogācāra schema enumerates the seven kinds of Prātimokṣa-restraint (bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, upāsaka, upāsikā). The clause 'taking the monastic restraint specifically' (3.4) signals that this whole chapter operates within the bhikṣu's full ordination, even though the underlying *śīla-skandha* is structurally broader.
sbh1.3:3.11: *Samyag-ratāḥ* is rendered 'properly engaged' in the conduct sections. The earlier 'rightly delighted' was too literal for the social-review context, where the list names those competent to judge whether a monk's deportment and duties conform to the world and Vinaya.
sbh1.3:5.14: *jñapti-caturtha karman* — the 'fourth-formal-motion act,' the standard Vinaya procedure by which full ordination is conferred. The proposer states the motion (*jñapti*) and then three times asks the assembled saṅgha to confirm; silence on all three counts conveys consent. The phrasing here makes the point that at ordination the candidate hears only the framework of the precepts — the full hundred-odd training rules are received under pledge (*samādāna-pratijñā*) and gradually awakened to over the course of training, which is the work of section 5 as a whole.
sbh1.3:8.6: *Nairyāṇika-śīla* — 'leading-out virtue,' i.e., virtue that leads out of saṁsāra. The text triangulates the three trainings: Prātimokṣa-restraint *is* the higher-virtue training (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), which serves as forerunner for the higher-mind (*adhicitta*) and higher-wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) trainings that complete the path. The term *nairyāṇika* recurs as the standard Yogācāra marker of soteriological efficacy.
sbh1.3:9.7: *Rājābhinirṇīta* / *caurābhinirṇīta* repeat the bad-going-forth motivation list from sbh1.1:12.14. Rendered 'under pressure from a king/thieves' rather than 'resolved upon' because the issue is external coercion or fear-driven renunciation, not a mental resolution.
sbh1.3:11.11: The printed/root *durmoṣa, durghara-jātīya* is suspect in this wrong-livelihood profile. The expected pair is the stock requisites-related description 'hard to satisfy / hard to support' (*durpoṣa/durbhara-jātīya*). The earlier English 'dull memory, bad-house lineage [duṣkulīna]' did not match the local root or the livelihood context, so the line is marked conjectural/corrupt.
sbh1.3:11.18: The root has *dhvāṅkṣa* ('crow/raven-like,' hence clamorous or cawing) plus *mukhara* ('talkative'). The prior bracket *bhāṇḍaka* was not local to this line and wrongly suggested flattery rather than noisy wrong-livelihood speech.
sbh1.3:11.20: In the wrong-livelihood speech section, *bhūta* is read as actual/real qualities, contrasted with qualities falsely attributed or inflated for gain. It is not 'past matters.' The passage is about manipulative self-presentation to induce donors, not historical narration.
sbh1.3:11.28: The list — *kuhanā* (hypocrisy), *lapanā* (talkative chatter), *naimittikatā* (insinuating hints), *naiṣpeṣikatā* (extortion / pressing), and *lābhena lābha-niścikīrṣā* (seeking gain by means of gain) — is the canonical *pañca-mithyā-jīva*, the five wrong livelihoods of monastics. Standard list across both Theravāda Visuddhimagga (I.61) and Sarvāstivāda-Yogācāra abhidharma; preserved here in brackets so the reader can recognize the technical taxonomy underneath the long descriptive expansions at 11.15–27.
sbh1.3:37.2: The three-fold danger schema (consumption / transformation / seeking, *pariniṣpatti / pariṇāma / paryeṣaṇa*) is a canonical Yogācāra analysis of food's faults. The seeking-danger then subdivides into six sub-types (37.31–35) — gathering, guarding, loss-of-affection, insatiability, lack-of-independence, misconduct — which structurally parallel the well-known *kāma-ādīnava* (drawbacks of sense-pleasures) lists in the Pāli Mahādukkhakkhandha-sutta (MN 13).
sbh1.3:39.2: The local Sanskrit is *asvātantrya* ('lack of autonomy / non-independence'), not *pāratantrya*. The English keeps the practical sense but the bracket now names the local term.
sbh1.3:42.20: The local root has *saṁgrahaḥ* and then a damaged/suspect *sāvadyaṁ dyaḥ*. The earlier bracket *samādāna* was not local. The English now follows *saṁgraha* as 'mental gathering' and marks the likely intended 'blameless' evaluation conjectural/corrupt, since printed *sāvadya* would mean blameworthy.
sbh1.3:39.48: The four kinds of food (*catur āhāra*) — morsel-made (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), contact (*sparśa*), mental volition (*manaḥsaṁcetanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) — is canonical abhidharma. The text narrows the *bhojane mātrajñatā* discussion to the first only, *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* — actual physical food taken by the body. The other three are subtle nutriments that sustain saṁsāric continuity at deeper levels.
sbh1.3:39.55: The formula here reads *na dravārtham*, not the more familiar *na darpārtham*. The local explanation at 39.57-58 explicitly glosses *drava* as sensual play/frivolity connected with lust and intercourse; English therefore uses 'frivolity' rather than 'arrogance' for this member of the food-reflection formula. *Mada* remains 'intoxication' in the next member.
sbh1.3:39.90: *aniṣṭha-prahāṇa* — literally 'abandonment by non-establishment.' The point is that for food, the practitioner does not abandon by ceasing-to-use (impossible while embodied); rather, he abandons attachment to it while continuing the physical act of eating. The phrase is technical: this is the same abandonment-without-cessation that recurs for the *requisite-items* (*pariṣkāra*) generally, where the bodily activity must continue but the affective grip on it must be released.
sbh1.3:40.90: *Bhojane samakārī* ('acting evenly with regard to food') is the local summary label at 40.90; *bhojane mātrajñatā* ('knowing the right measure in food') names the larger requisite at 40.121. The measure is glossed concretely by the analysis at 40.59-74: balanced (*sama*) versus unbalanced (*viṣama*) eating, where balanced cuts across four dimensions — quantity (not too little, not too much), digestibility, wholesomeness, and freedom-from-defilement-in-procurement. The Vinaya formula *paryāptaṁ* (sufficient) and *yathāpramāṇa* (according to measure) point to the same idea.
sbh1.3:42.6: The printed/extracted line is noisy around *sāyāhnaṁ ardharātraḥ ... sāyāhnaṁ*, but the functional definition is clear from the following words: the early watch begins at sunset and occupies the first part of the night, a little more than one watch. The late watch is defined separately at 42.165-166.
sbh1.3:42.31: The obscuring-dharmas list here follows the standard hindrance-food pattern: attractiveness-perception feeds sense-desire, the resistance-sign feeds ill-will, darkness feeds sloth-and-torpor, and so on. The extracted *a śubhatā* is therefore read contextually as *śubhatā* ('attractiveness'), not *aśubhatā* ('unattractiveness'), which would be an antidote rather than an obscuring condition.
sbh1.3:42.57: *Kāmaniyanti* belongs to the sense-lust cluster (*kāmarāga, kāmacchanda, kāmālaya, kāmaniyanti, kāmādhyavasāna*). It is a binding/compulsion toward sensuality, not sense-restraint. The English now keeps the sequence as sense-lust, sense-desire, sensual attachment, sensual compulsion, and sensual fixation.
sbh1.3:42.104: The three *ādhipateyya* (predominances) — dharma-, self-, and world-predominance — is a canonical Yogācāra schema applied to motivation for abandoning the hindrances. Dharma-predominance (42.21–103) is the practitioner's own analytical work with antidotes; self-predominance (42.106–109) is the motive of self-respect ('let me not be known as a hindrance-maker'); world-predominance (42.110–117) is the motive of accountability before the Teacher, the deities, the wise, and the saṅgha. The threefold framework reappears in the Yogācārabhūmi as the standard motivational analysis whenever a single practice has multiple subjective angles.
sbh1.3:42.36: The local term is *āloka-nimitta* ('light-sign'), not *āloka-saṁjñā* ('perception of light'). The latter is a related practice term elsewhere, but here the practitioner has grasped a sign, so the bracket follows the root.
sbh1.3:42.185: The four *samyak-prayoga* (right tasks) of wakefulness-yoga — sustained wholesome practice while awake, sleeping at the right time, sleeping with undefiled mind, [and] waking at the right time — are paired (42.196–213) one-to-one with the four phrases of the canonical wakefulness-formula (purifies-by-walking-and-sitting / lies-down-foot-on-foot / mindful-and-fully-aware / wakes-in-the-last-watch). This pairing is a Yogācāra hermeneutic technique: a brief sūtra-formula is fully unfolded by mapping each phrase onto a named element of a corresponding doctrinal list.
sbh1.3:43.1: *saṁprajāna-vihāritā* (dwelling-with-full-awareness) is introduced here as the next major topic (paragraphs 43–47): the practitioner's continuous knowing of bodily and mental activity across the full waking day. Sets up the breakdown into *abhikrama / pratikrama* and the larger nine-pair list of postures and activities that follows.
sbh1.3:44.22: *Svalakṣaṇa* in the full-awareness section is rendered as 'specific characteristic,' matching the project's broader technical usage in the vipaśyanā and skill-object chapters. The earlier 'own-marks' was literal but inconsistent and less readable.
sbh1.3:45.1: *Dhāraṇa* covers both wearing robes and carrying the bowl. The English therefore uses 'wearing/carrying' rather than the mechanical 'bearing,' which produced unreadable phrases such as 'bowl-bearing should be borne' while adding no philological precision.
sbh1.3:45.7: *Ādhiṣṭhānika cīvara* is rendered as 'determined robe,' i.e. a robe formally determined for use, not a 'base-cloth.' The adjacent *atireka-cīvara vikalpanārha* is an extra robe fit for assignment/designation; the translation keeps the Vinaya register without inventing a misleading English category.
sbh1.3:45.34: The food taxonomy distinguishes the broad category *aśita* ('eaten' / alms-food use), then divides it into *khādita* ('chewed,' eaten but not drunk) and *svādita* ('tasted,' items treated as eaten and also drunk). This is a Vinaya-style use-classification, not a modern nutrition taxonomy; the English avoids the compressed and misleading 'eaten-but-not-drunk' compound.
sbh1.3:47.13: The sitting definition uses the same *pratimukhī smṛti* formula as sbh3.0:1.170-175. Rendered consistently as 'mindfulness to the fore,' not the earlier 'facing forward' or the mechanical 'fronting-before.'
sbh1.3:52.10: The printed/root order of the brahmavihāras is *maitrī, karuṇā, upekṣā, muditā*. The English follows the standard meditative order *maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā* but now marks the reordered pair conjectural/corrupt so the repair is not silent.
sbh1.3:48.1: Although the chapter heading at 43.1 introduces *saṁprajāna-vihāritā*, paragraphs 48–55 actually open the next saṁbhāra — *kalyāṇa-mitratā* (association with good friends) — by detailing the conduct on the alms-round and in solitary practice (47–50) and then enumerating the eight qualities (51–52) and four roles (53) of the good friend himself, closing with the summary at 54.1. The two topics are bridged because what one learns through *saṁprajāna* in daily activity is precisely the conduct *modeled* by the *kalyāṇa-mitra*.
sbh1.3:48.9: *Ghoṣa* is a cowherd settlement or encampment, not a brothel; the prostitute/prostitute's house is the following item, *veśya*. The list names unsuitable places for alms-round approach: cowherd settlement, tavern, prostitute's house, royal household, and caṇḍāla quarter.
sbh1.3:49.3: The phrase is read as *manasikāra-anugata* ('accompanied by attention'), not *a-manasikāra* ('non-attention'). In this full-awareness/alms-round context the practitioner is applied to the wholesome side with attention and inward-turned faculties; 'non-attention' would undermine the practice instruction.
sbh1.3:52.7: The four-fold characterization of the good friend — much-learned (*bahuśruta*), attainer (*samāpatti-lābhin*), compassionate (*kṛpālu*), and of unwearying mind (*akhinna-mānasa*) — followed by patience, confidence, and speech-faculty at 51.25–52.11, yields the eight causes/aspects named at 52.12 and again at 53.51. This same eight-fold list is canonical for *kalyāṇa-mitra* across Yogācāra sources. The 'three wonders' at 51.12–13 (*prātihārya*: psychic power, mind-reading, admonition) match the standard Pāli list of *iddhi/ādesanā/anuśāsanī*-pāṭihāriya from DN 11 and elsewhere.
sbh1.3:52.21: This is the standard teaching sequence *sandarśaka, samādāpaka, samuttejaka, saṁpraharṣaka*: one who demonstrates, exhorts, arouses, and gladdens. The prior 'shower of delight' misread *saṁdarśaka* as if it were connected with delight rather than showing/demonstrating.
sbh1.3:54.31: The list of twelve *kathā-vastu* (topics of discourse) — virtue-talk, wisdom-talk, liberation-talk, few-desires-talk, knowing-and-seeing-of-liberation-talk, contentment-talk, abandonment-talk, dispassion-talk, cessation-talk, decrease-talk [*apacaya*], non-mixing-talk [*asaṁsarga*], pratītyasamutpāda-conforming-talk — is the canonical *dvādaśa-kathā-vastu* of Yogācāra abhidharma. Cf. the ten-fold *kathā-vatthu* list in the Pāli Anguttara (AN 10.69).
sbh1.3:54.46: The line introduces talk connected with the four noble truths but the extracted root reads *phalam vā* after suffering, origin, and cessation. Context requires the fourth truth, *mārga* ('path'); English marks the repair as conjectural/corrupt rather than silently translating the impossible 'fruit' as the fourth truth.
sbh1.3:74.60: The twelve (or thirteen) *dhutaguṇa* — *paiṇḍapātika, sāpadāna-cārin, aikāsanika, khalupaścādbhaktika, traicīvarika, nāmatika, pāṁsukūlika, āraṇyaka, vṛkṣamūlika, ābhyavakāśika, śmāśānika, naiṣadika, yāthāsaṁstarika* — match the Pāli *dhutaṅga* list of the Visuddhimagga II, with terminology and ordering essentially identical. The Yogācāra count of thirteen treats *piṇḍapāta* and *sāpadāna-cāra* as distinct; the count of twelve subsumes the second under the first. The functional analysis at 80.1–16 maps each dhutaguṇa onto the specific kind of lust (*rāga*) it counteracts — a Yogācāra abhidharma move that converts the ascetic list from a catalogue of practices into a typology of antidotes.
sbh1.3:79.10: The folk-etymology *dhuta-guṇa* ← *dhuta* (shaken, shaken-off): just as wool/cotton becomes loose and workable when shaken, so the mind becomes loose and workable when 'shaken' free of attachment to food, robes, and lodging through these ascetic disciplines. The simile is also found in the Visuddhimagga and is the standard explanation across Buddhist sects for why these are called 'dhutaguṇa.'
sbh1.3:80.71: The printed/root *tena cātmadaṁ vā nyī cī varaṁ dhārayati* is visibly corrupt, but *cīvaraṁ dhārayati* is recoverable. The English gives the likely functional sense, 'wears a self-disciplining robe,' treating the phrase as related to self-taming (*ātma-dama*) and marking the line conjectural/corrupt rather than preserving the unresolved vow/robe slash hedge.
sbh1.3:80.98: The printed/root *avavādavastuprāvṛtaḥ* is likely corrupt in the ornament simile. The surrounding sequence is the stock image of a young man 'bathed and anointed, clothed, adorned with ornaments'; the expected phrase is probably *avadāta-vastra-prāvṛtaḥ* ('clothed in clean/bright garments') or a close equivalent. The previous 'approved [/finely-chosen] clothing' read *avavāda* as approval/instruction and does not fit the simile. The English is therefore marked conjectural/corrupt.
sbh1.3:80.48: The *ṣaṭ-sāmīcī-dharma* (six conciliatory dharmas) — friendly bodily action, friendly verbal action, friendly mental action, sharing in gains (open-eating at meals), sharing in virtue [*śīla-sāmānyatā*], and sharing in view [*dṛṣṭi-sāmānyatā*] — are the standard list of the six *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (Pāli) / *sāmīcī-dharma* (Skt.) of conciliatory living. Identical in Pāli AN 6.11–12 and across Yogācāra sources, defining the conditions of harmonious *saṅgha* life.
sbh1.3:80.57: *Saṁgraha-śīla* here describes an approachable, welcoming disposition in the definition of being lovely (*peśala*). The previous bracket *pūrva-saṅgāhika* was not local to the line. *Ātta-santāna* at 78.58 is taken functionally as composed or gathered bearing, rather than the literal but opaque 'well-bound continuum.'
sbh1.3:80.25: The extracted root reads *etenātmānam utkarṣayati | parāṁś ca paṁsayati* without negators, but that would make this a self-exalting, other-disparaging person precisely in the definition of being endowed with the dharmas of noble persons. The expected reading is *na ... na ...*; English restores the negative sense and marks the line [Damaged/Conjectural].
sbh1.3:80.97: The closing simile — the well-adorned young man — picks up and inverts the *ornament*-simile from 12.22–29 (where virtue is contrasted with worldly ornaments that fail in old age and misfortune): there, worldly ornaments fail and only virtue endures; here, the worldly ornament *succeeds* as a comparison-vehicle precisely because the disciple's recluse-ornament is its true, non-decaying analogue. The two passages function as inclusio at the opening and close of the saṁbhāra-section.
sbh1.3:86.1: Closing colophon for the entire Yogasthāna I — not just the naiṣkramyabhūmi. The Sanskrit accusative *prathamaṁ yogasthānaṁ* leaves the verb implicit (*samāptam*, 'is completed'); rendered here with a bracketed gloss. The same colophon-form repeats at the close of YS II, III, and IV in the source.
sbh1.3:32.17: The four-term cluster *nityakāritā / sātatya-kāritā / niryāṇa-kāritā / satkṛtya-kāritā* — 'constant action / continual action / action toward going-forth / action done with respect' — pairs each term in the question (32.15–16) with its definitional synonym (32.17–18). The Sanskrit *iyam ucyate X* construction here re-glosses the question's term, so 'constant' is *defined as* 'continual' and 'going-forth' is *defined as* 'with-respect'. Translation makes the pairing explicit so the reader can see the gloss structure rather than reading 32.17–18 as separate vague claims.
sbh1.3:32.38: *samāvasthā-avacāraka* — literally 'one who explores / operates within an even state.' Rendered here as 'one who maintains a balanced state.' The earlier draft used 'acting in the state of equipoise,' which is technically defensible but sounded liturgical; 'balanced state' carries the same conceptual content with less ornament. Distinct from *upekṣā* (equanimity) proper — *upekṣā* names the affective neutrality, *samāvasthā-avacāraka* names the stable mode of operating from within it.
sbh1.3:35.2: The response to arisen unwholesome dharmas is positive, not negative: *adhivāsayati, prajahāti, viśodhayati, vyantīkaroti* means he withstands/endures them, abandons them, purifies them, and puts an end to them. The prior 'does not accommodate them' inserted a negation not present in the Sanskrit.
sbh1.3:35.50: The twofold distinction here is doctrinally important: *pratisaṁkhyāna-bala* (the power of reflective discrimination) is the analytical force that *recognizes* danger in sense-objects without yet uprooting it; *bhāvanā-bala* (the power of cultivation) actually uproots the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) at its karmic root. The first kind belongs to the path of requisites (*saṁbhāra-mārga*) — pre-realization. The second is operative within the dispassion-stage proper, i.e., from the path of seeing onward.
sbh1.3:56.16: *geya* (sung-verse) and *vyākaraṇa* (predictive teaching) are paired in 56.16–20 with two contrasting kinds of sūtra: *neyārtha* (meaning-to-be-interpreted) sūtras paired with *geya*, and *nītārtha* (definitive-meaning) sūtras paired with *vyākaraṇa*. The pairing is structural and tradition-recognized in the twelve-aṅga schema; preserved here in brackets for visibility.
sbh1.3:61.2: The adbhuta-dharma audience list is restored as the standard fourfold-plus-training community: monks, nuns, female probationers, male and female novices, male and female lay-followers. The extracted root is compressed/noisy around *śrāmaṇera/śrāmaṇerī/upāsaka/upāsikā*, but omitting female novices and male lay-followers would make the community list asymmetrical.
sbh1.3:62.4: The mapping of the twelve *aṅgas* (verbal genres) onto the three *piṭakas* (baskets) given here is a Yogācāra schema: ten aṅgas (sūtra through adbhutadharma) constitute the *sūtra-piṭaka*; *nidāna* alone constitutes the *vinaya-piṭaka* (since vinaya rules are framed by their occasioning narratives); *upadeśa* constitutes the *abhidharma-piṭaka*. Different traditions (Theravāda, etc.) assign these differently.
sbh1.3:62.30: The six *acintya-sthāna* (unthinkable matters) — self, being, world, the karmic results of beings, the meditator's range as known to meditators, and the Buddha's range as known to Buddhas — are explicitly *set aside* before reflection begins. The reflection that constitutes *cintanā* operates on what *can* be analytically known: dharma's own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general-characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
sbh1.3:63.2: The four reasonings (*yukti*) introduced at 62.44 — *apekṣā* (dependence), *kāryakāraṇa* (cause-effect), *upapatti-sādhana* (demonstration-of-arising), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) — are a canonical Yogācāra fourfold, expanded in section 63. Compare the four-reasoning treatment in [sbh3.2](sbh3.2.html#sbh3.2:0.2) (vipaśyanā), where they reappear as the analytical engines of insight.
sbh1.3:63.25: The proof list at 63.23 names five characteristics of the aggregates: impermanent, dependently arisen, suffering, empty, and non-self. The summary at 63.25 explicitly includes impermanence, dependent-arising, suffering, and emptiness; non-self is supplied in English to keep the summary aligned with the proposition list immediately above.
sbh1.3:64.4: *anantarāya* is defined here by negation: the discussion (64.7–64.30) details the *obstacles* (*antarāya*); *non-obstacle* is then implied as their absence. This negative-definition pattern is common in the Śrāvakabhūmi when the positive content has already been laid out elsewhere or is best understood by contrast.
sbh1.3:65.2: The threefold division of obstacle is structurally important: *prayoga-antarāya* obstructs the *application* itself (illness, lack of basic requisites); *prāvivekya-antarāya* obstructs the *seclusion* in which application happens (busy-ness, sociability, distraction); *pratisaṁlayana-antarāya* obstructs *retreat* — the inner work of śamatha and vipaśyanā — through heedlessness, premature settling, self-aggrandizement, or fickleness. The categories cascade from gross-and-environmental to subtle-and-internal.
sbh1.3:66.3: The six-question framework — who, to whom, what, by what, how, why — is the standard Yogācāra analytical schema applied to any practice (also visible in the *kena/kiṁ/kutaḥ/kathaṁ* framing of indriya-saṁvara at 35.16–18). Sections 65–70 answer each question in turn: 65 = giver-and-recipients; 67–69 = the thing given (sentient and non-sentient); 70 = means, manner, motive.
sbh1.3:67.3: *dātṛ* (giver) and *dāna-pati* (patron) are distinguished: anyone whose own thing is given is a giver; the patron is specifically the one who gives *willingly*. The distinction matters because one can be a giver under coercion (e.g., taxation, theft) without being a patron; only the willing giver is a patron, and only the willing giving constitutes the *tyāga* requisite.
sbh1.3:69.8: Self-giving (offering parts of one's own body — head, hand, flesh, blood) is here explicitly *bracketed off* as a bodhisattva practice that is not the *tyāga* requisite intended in the śrāvakabhūmi context. This is one of the few places where the source explicitly demarcates between śrāvaka and bodhisattva paths within a discussion that could apply to either.
sbh1.3:74.53: The ascetic-quality list now brackets local forms rather than importing parallel/normalized labels: *piṇḍapātika*, *sāvadāna-piṇḍapātika*, *ekāsanika*, and *naiṣadyika*. The sequential alms-food taker corresponds functionally to the better-known *sāpadāna-cārin*, but the bracket follows the local line.
sbh1.3:80.3: The ascetic-quality antidote list at 80.1–16 now avoids slash-hedges where the Sanskrit is straightforward: *praṇīta-cīvara-rāga* is rendered consistently as lust for fine robes, not differentiated as 'soft' versus 'many' robes without local evidence. The compound *pārśva-sukha-śayana-sukha-rāga* is likewise two coordinated comforts, not a side/lying alternative. At 80.11 the root has *saṁsarga-rāga* ('association-lust'), not the preceding *saṁsparśa-rāga* ('contact-lust'), matching the forest-dweller's withdrawal from social association. Similarly, *varṇa* at 40.20 is complexion, *dhārayati* at 75.11 is keeping more than three robes, and *apratigupta-bhojī* at 80.45 is eating openly as a sharer.
sbh1.3:74.63: The printed/extracted *veśyānuveśya-kulāni* is treated as corrupt or noisy in the sequential alms-food context. The practice being defined is the house-to-house alms round (*sāvadāna/sāpadāna*), not approach to prostitute families; English therefore marks the line conjectural/corrupt and renders the functional sense 'from house to house, from family to family.'
sbh1.3:42.67: Restored from PDF 1401-1404. sbh1.3:78.5: Restored from PDF 2313-2314.
